sections.title: The country
sections.subtitle: The world’s largest state, spanning Europe and Asia

paragraphs: Russia is the largest country in the world, stretching from Eastern Europe across northern Asia. Throughout its history it has been a major political, military and cultural power. Today, however, it is overshadowed by the controversy surrounding its invasion of Ukraine.

sections.title: Recent history
sections.subtitle: Empire, Soviet Union and Russian Federation

paragraphs: Russia underwent dramatic changes: from an authoritarian tsarist monarchy to the dominant republic of the communist Soviet Union, and finally to the independent Russian Federation. This encompassed two world wars, revolution, civil war and the Cold War.

In the 21st century, Russia recovered from the instability of the 1990s, aided by its vast energy revenues, while Vladimir Putin centralised power and restricted political opposition. Its increasingly assertive foreign policy culminated in the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

sections.title: Football origins
sections.subtitle: From British expatriate clubs to the Soviet and Russian league systems

entries.heading: The first press-reported match
paragraphs: Football reached imperial Russia through British merchants, engineers and sailors in port cities. The first match reported by the Russian press was staged in Saint Petersburg: Vasilyevsky Island’s largely British side defeated the Circle of Sports Enthusiasts 6–0.

The translated contemporary report describes football as an English invention, lists three early Saint Petersburg clubs and notes that Vasilyevsky Island wore blue while its opponents wore white. The reporter found the calls of “foul”, “hands” and “out” bewildering, remarked on the physical play and ended by predicting that, with more training, the Russians would catch up with the English.

entries.heading: The first organised leagues
paragraphs: In 1901, three expatriate clubs formed the Saint Petersburg Football League, Russia’s first organised competition. The game then spread through schools, factories and local leagues. By 1913 Moscow’s league alone contained 25 teams, while as many as ten local leagues had been created.

entries.heading: Football reorganised by the Soviet state
paragraphs: War, revolution and civil war broke the imperial structure. The Bolsheviks made old clubs re-register as proletarian organisations, while new teams became associated with the state apparatus: Dynamo with the secret police, CDKA/CSKA with the army and Lokomotiv with the railways.

entries.heading: Spartak and the Starostin brothers
paragraphs: In 1934 Nikolai Starostin and his brothers created Spartak Moscow, named after Spartacus, the Roman slave turned rebel. It quickly became the “people’s team” and the most successful club in Russian history.

Spartak’s success made the brothers political targets. They were sent to a Siberian labour camp, although some says Spartak-supporting guards treated them well. Starostin is also credited as the main force behind the creation of the Soviet Top League in 1936, the first regular national league.

entries.heading: Russian clubs in the Soviet league
paragraphs: Among Russian clubs, Spartak won 12 Soviet league titles, Dynamo Moscow 11 and CSKA seven. Zenit Leningrad’s 1984 triumph was its only Soviet league championship.
Internationally, Spartak reached the 1990/91 European Cup semi-finals after eliminating Real Madrid.

entries.heading: A new federation and Spartak’s dominance
paragraphs: After the USSR dissolved in 1991, the Russian Football Union was formed in February 1992 and a new national league began that year. Spartak won nine of the first ten Russian championships from 1992 to 2001; Alania interrupted the run in 1995.
Spartak also reached the 1993 Cup Winners’ Cup semi-finals and the 1998 UEFA Cup semi-finals.

entries.heading: The Premier League and European trophies
paragraphs: The leading clubs created a separately run Premier League in 2001, first played in 2002. Between 2002 and 2010, Lokomotiv, CSKA, Zenit and Rubin Kazan all won championships, ending Spartak’s one-club rule.
CSKA won the 2005 UEFA Cup, the first European trophy won by a Russian club. Zenit won the UEFA Cup and UEFA Super Cup in 2008.
Zenit later won six consecutive domestic championships from 2018/19 through 2023/24. Krasnodar claimed its first title in 2024/25, before Zenit regained the championship on the final day of 2025/26.

cards.title: Russian Premier League
cards.text: The Premier League is the 16-club top division. Below it are the professional First and Second Leagues. Because of Russia’s immense size, lower divisions are increasingly split into regional groups to reduce travel distances and costs.

cards.title: Кубок России
cards.text: The national knockout competition is open to amateur clubs through the Federal Subjects’ championships, similar to the FA Cup. Its table lists CSKA and Lokomotiv as the most successful clubs, with nine wins each.

cards.title: Суперкубок России
cards.text: The league champions face the Russian Cup winners. Zenit is the record holder with nine wins, followed by CSKA with eight.

cards.title: Zenit Saint Petersburg
cards.text: Arguably Russia’s most successful club of recent years, highlighting its domestic dominance and its 2008 UEFA Cup and UEFA Super Cup victories.

cards.title: Spartak Moscow
cards.text: Spartak is presented as the traditional club with Russia’s strongest fan base and as the defining force of the first decade of the independent Russian championship.

cards.title: CSKA Moscow
cards.text: CSKA is identified as one of the country’s oldest major clubs. Its 2005 UEFA Cup victory is highlighted as a landmark for Russian club football.

sections.title: National team
sections.subtitle: Imperial Russia, the USSR, the CIS and independent Russia through suspension

entries.heading: Imperial Russia’s official debut
paragraphs: Imperial Russia made its official international debut at the Stockholm Olympics, losing 2–1 to Finland. The next day, Germany won 16–0 in the consolation tournament, still one of Olympic football’s largest victories.
Imperial Russia played eight official internationals and won none before the 1917 Revolution.

entries.heading: From the Russian Soviet Republic to the USSR
paragraphs: Following the Civil War, the Russian Soviet Republic made its debut against the Finnish Workers’ Sports Federation, a breakaway workers’ team.

After the Soviet Union was formed in 1922, the Russian Soviet team gave way to the USSR national side. Soviet football remained largely isolated from mainstream international competition until its Olympic debut at Helsinki in 1952.

entries.heading: Olympic champions and World Cup debut
paragraphs: The USSR won Olympic gold at Melbourne 1956, beating Yugoslavia 1–0 in the final. Two years later it entered its first World Cup in Sweden, defeated England in a group play-off and then lost to the hosts in the quarter-finals.

entries.heading: Europe’s first champions
paragraphs: In 1960 the USSR became Europe’s first champion, defeating Yugoslavia 2–1 after extra time in Paris. Goalkeeper Lev Yashin anchored the side; in 1963 he became—and remains—the only goalkeeper to win the Ballon d’Or.
At the 1962 World Cup, the USSR again lost to the host nation, Chile, in the quarter-finals.

entries.heading: European finals and the 1966 World Cup peak
paragraphs: The USSR lost the 1964 European final to hosts Spain, but reached its World Cup peak in 1966. Victories over North Korea, Italy, Chile and Hungary carried the team into the semi-finals; defeats by West Germany and Portugal left it fourth. The USSR also finished fourth at Euro 1968.

The USSR lost a World Cup quarter-final to Uruguay in 1970. Until the 1970s, Russian clubs had previously supplied most Soviet internationals, during that decade and after, the centre of Soviet football increasingly shifted towards Ukraine.

entries.heading: The temporary CIS team
paragraphs: Following the dissolution of the Soviet Union, a temporary Commonwealth of Independent States team was created to fulfil the USSR’s remaining sporting commitments. It represented the former Soviet republics at UEFA Euro 1992 but did not advance from the group stage.

entries.heading: Independent Russia and Salenko’s record
paragraphs: Independent Russia’s first World Cup ended in the group stage. Oleg Salenko nevertheless made history by scoring five goals in a 6–1 victory over Cameroon—the record for one player in a World Cup match.
His six goals across the tournament earned him a shared Golden Boot.

entries.heading: Opening-round exits and missed tournaments
paragraphs: Russia qualified for UEFA Euro 1996 but failed to progress beyond the group stage. It then missed both the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2000.
Russia returned for the 2002 World Cup and Euro 2004, but was again eliminated in the opening round on both occasions.

entries.heading: The Euro 2008 semi-final
paragraphs: Russia missed the 2006 and 2010 World Cups. Its best result since independence came at Euro 2008, where it reached the semi-finals before losing 3–0 to eventual champions Spain.
The team returned for Euro 2012, the 2014 World Cup and Euro 2016, but exited in the group stage each time.

entries.heading: World Cup hosts
paragraphs: FIFA awarded Russia the 2018 World Cup. The tournament drove construction or major renovation across eleven host cities, including Moscow, Saint Petersburg, Kazan, Sochi, Samara, Volgograd, Saransk and Kaliningrad.
The host team exceeded expectations and reached the quarter-finals.

entries.heading: Suspension from FIFA and UEFA competitions
paragraphs: After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, FIFA and UEFA suspended every Russian national team and club from their competitions until further notice.
Russia missed the 2022 World Cup play-offs and has since played only friendlies internationally.

sections.title: Historical line-up
sections.subtitle: An entirely subjective 4-2-3-1
sections.intro: The continuation selects an all-time side composed of players from Imperial, Soviet and independent Russian football.

players.name: Lev Yashin
players.description: The Black Spider, the only goalkeeper to win the Ballon d’Or and considered one of the greatest ever.

players.name: Vladimir Ponomaryov
players.description: A powerful and reliable CSKA defender.

players.name: Anatoli Bashashkin
players.description: Renowned for his long-range passing and physical strength.

players.name: Albert Shesternyov
players.description: “Ivan the Terrible”, captain in the 1960s and considered the best Russian defender.

players.name: Valery Voronin
players.description: One of the most complete midfielders of the 1960s.

players.name: Igor Netto
players.description: Captain when the USSR won Olympic gold in 1956 and the inaugural European Championship in 1960.

players.name: Igor Chislenko
players.description: A fast, direct Dynamo Moscow winger.

players.name: Fyodor Cherenkov
players.description: Perhaps the most naturally gifted Russian playmaker, celebrated for his vision, control and combination play.

players.name: Andrey Arshavin
players.description: The most outstanding attacking player of independent Russia.

players.name: Eduard Streltsov
players.description: A powerful and extraordinarily creative forward whose back-heel passes became known in Russia as the Streltsov pass.

recordGroups.title: Match records
items: First match: Russia 2–0 Mexico, Moscow, 16 August 1992.
Biggest victory: Russia 11–0 Brunei, friendly, 15 November 2024.
Biggest competitive victory: Russia 9–0 San Marino, Euro qualifier, 8 June 2019.
Heaviest defeat: Portugal 7–1 Russia, World Cup qualifier, 13 October 2004.
